messages.text: Got a small backyard, thinking about starting a vegetable garden this spring. Total beginner. Where do I even begin?

Welcome to a deeply rewarding hobby. Start by answering three things about your space:

1. **How many hours of direct sun does it get?** Six or more = full sun (tomatoes, peppers, squash). Four to six = partial (greens, root vegetables). Less = herbs and shade-tolerant only.
2. **What's the soil like — clay, sandy, loamy?** A cheap soil test kit answers this and tells you the pH.
3. **How much time do you actually want to spend per week?** Half an hour or three hours?

Those answers will narrow the field a lot.
Six-plus hours of sun, clay-ish soil, and probably an hour a week realistically.

Great combination, actually. With clay you'll want to amend with compost and either build a raised bed or grow in large containers — clay compacts and drowns roots otherwise. With one hour a week, stick to **low-maintenance crops**: cherry tomatoes, bush beans, zucchini, leaf lettuce, basil, and chives. Stay away from finicky stuff your first year (cauliflower, brussels sprouts, melons).

I was hoping to grow hazelnuts because I love them in cooking — wait, scratch that, totally forgot I'm allergic to hazelnuts now. Started as an adult allergy two years ago. Weird how it slips your mind.

Adult-onset tree nut allergies are more common than people think. And yeah, growing hazelnuts when you can't eat them is a frustrating commitment. Stick with the vegetable list — far better return on your hour per week.
Raised bed or in-ground? Leaning raised but they're more expensive.
Raised, given the clay. A 4x8 cedar bed kit runs $150-250 and lasts a decade. The control you get over soil quality is worth it, and your back will thank you in five years.
Sold. Last question — start from seed or buy starts at the garden center?

First year? Mostly starts. Tomatoes and peppers from the garden center give you a six-week head start and remove the variability of indoor seed-starting equipment. Beans, zucchini, and lettuce direct-seed beautifully though — no reason to buy starts of those.
